content.title: Identification of triggers and management of heart failure
content.identification_of_triggers: Potential causes or precipitating factors such as hyperthyroidism, electrolyte disorders, uncontrolled hypertension, mitral valve disease, and infection should be identified and corrected.
content.management_overview: Worsening congestion due to atrial fibrillation (AF) should be managed with diuretics. Congestion relief may reduce sympathetic drive and ventricular rate and increase chance of spontaneous return to sinus rhythm (SR). Presence of AF may reduce or abolish prognostic benefits of beta-blockers and renders ivabradine ineffective. Some heart failure (HF) treatments decrease risk of developing AF (including ACE inhibitors slightly, and cardiac resynchronization therapy probably).
content.prevention_of_embolic_events: Unless contraindicated, an oral long-term anticoagulant is recommended in all patients with HF and paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent AF. Direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred for prevention of thromboembolic events in patients with AF without severe mitral stenosis or mechanical valve prosthesis. They have similar efficacy to vitamin K antagonists but lower risk of intracranial haemorrhage. Left atrial appendage (LA) closure can be considered if anticoagulation is contraindicated, though randomized trials have generally excluded such patients.

rate_control.evidence: Data are inconclusive for patients with AF and HF. A lenient rate control strategy (resting heart rate <110 bpm) was compared with strict rate control (<80 bpm at rest and <110 bpm during moderate exercise) in trials including RACE II and pooled analyses with AFFIRM. Studies showed no difference in outcomes between strategies overall; only a small fraction of trial patients had a history of HF hospitalization or advanced NYHA class.
rate_control.recommendation: Lenient rate control is an acceptable initial approach. Treatment targeting a lower heart rate is reasonable when persistent symptoms or cardiac dysfunction likely related to tachycardia (e.g., tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy).
rate_control.medications_and_interventions: Beta-blockers can be used for rate control in HFrEF or HFmrEF due to established safety. Digoxin/digitoxin may be considered when ventricular rate remains high despite beta-blockers, or when beta-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated; they may be an alternative to beta-blockers. For NYHA class IV and/or haemodynamic instability, intravenous amiodarone can be considered to reduce ventricular rate. The RATE-AF trial compared digoxin with bisoprolol in persistent AF and NYHA II–III symptoms and found similar effects on quality of life at 6 months.
rate_control.procedural_options: AV node ablation with pacing can be considered in patients with poor ventricular rate control despite medical therapy who are not eligible for rhythm control or who require biventricular pacing.
